EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A winter storm brought ice, sleet and extreme cold to southeast Texas from the 24th through the 26th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A winter storm moved into southeast Texas on the night of the 24th. Precipitation began on the night of the 24th, when the College Station ASOS station KCLL measured a trace of Freezing Rain. Sleet occurred overnight with a trained storm spotter measuring around 0.1 inches of sleet early on the morning of the 24th. Not long after, a local emergency manager reported very slick conditions across College Station and Bryan, including along Highway 6 and OSR. Later that morning, a trained storm spotter shared a photo on social media showing ice accumulations. In the photo, around 0.25 inches of flat ice and 0.125 inches of radial ice was measured.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A winter storm brought ice, sleet and extreme cold to southeast Texas from the 24th through the 26th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A winter storm moved into southeast Texas on the night of the 24th. After the storm cleared the next day, Trinity county Sheriffs Office reported that bridges had been iced over across the county. One person had also reportedly slid off the road as a result.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong arctic cold front moved across west Texas and southeast New Mexico during the afternoon and evening hours of the 23rd. Meanwhile, a potent upper-level trough neared the region from the west. Widespread rain began during the morning of the 23rd in western portions of the area and gradually transitioned eastward through the day. As the front moved across the area, rain transitioned to sleet and snow from north to south (with freezing rain being more common south of the Pecos River and in the Davis Mountains). Off and on bands of sleet and snow continued across the Permian Basin and southeast New Mexico on the 24th, and became mostly snow by the 25th before moving east of the area late in the afternoon. Snowfall/sleet totals reached winter storm criteria across much of the northern basin and in southeast New Mexico. Lower snow and ice totals were reported further south.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A member of the public reported 0.1 inch of ice due to heavy freezing rain. Thunder was reported and GLM satellite imagery showed cloud-to-cloud lightning during the time of the report. The total duration of the winter weather event is estimated from AWOS data and radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Across South Texas and the Coastal Bend, persistent dry conditions through late January led to worsening drought and critically low soil moisture, limiting agricultural progress and stressing rangeland. Periods of unseasonably warm weather were followed by hard freezes and a winter storm, though precipitation was generally limited, with only modest rainfall of up to around an inch in parts of the Coastal Bend providing minor short-term improvement to soil moisture. Producers largely completed field preparation but delayed spring planting due to insufficient moisture for germination. Winter pastures and forage growth struggled under the dry conditions, resulting in poor to fair range conditions and increased reliance on hay and supplemental feed for livestock. While citrus and cool-season vegetable harvests continued, drought stress remained a concern for crop development and pasture recovery, and additional rainfall will be needed to improve soil moisture and support the upcoming planting season.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Continued D2 and D3 drought. D3 expanded to cover whole county on 1/13.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The I-35 Corridor, Rio Grande and Coastal Plains received less than normal precipitation during the month, and the drought worsened or remained unchanged. Caldwell, Fayette, Guadalupe, Hays, Lavaca, Maverick, Travis, and Zavala Counties went from Severe (D2) Drought category to Extreme (D3) Drought. Williamson County went from Moderate (D1) Drought to D2. Atascosa, Bastrop, Bexar, Comal, De Witt, Dimmit, Frio, Gonzales, Karnes, Lee, Medina, and Wilson Counties remained in D3. Blanco, Kendall, and Kinney remained in D2. The Edwards Aquifer level was unchanged but was still 39.1 feet below normal. Area reservoirs were below normal conservation levels. Lake Travis dropped 0.5 feet and was 13.8 feet below normal. Canyon Lake dropped 0.6 feet and was 21.0 feet below normal. The 7-day average streamflow was much below (<10%) normal on the Lavaca, Blanco, San Marcos, lower Guadalupe, Medina, lower Nueces, and Atascosa Rivers, and below (10%-24%) normal on the San Gabriel, Colorado, upper Guadalupe, San Antonio, and Frio Rivers. Most water providers encouraged conservation while San Antonio and Universal City imposed stage 3 restrictions and New Braunfels and Austin had stage 2. Of the counties in D2 or worse drought, Atascosa, Bastrop, Blanco, Bexar, Caldwell, Comal, De Witt, Dimmit, Fayette, Frio, Guadalupe, Hays, Karnes, Medina, Wilson, and Zavala had outdoor burn bans in effect at the end of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A classic winter weather pattern setup across the region with an upper low moving through northwest Mexico while a back door cold front moved into Hudspeth County. Southwest flow aloft ahead of the upper low kept some warm air aloft over the area and the eastern Hudspeth County experienced a period of freezing rain with over a half inch reported around Dell City.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Rio Grande Electric Cooperative reported power outages around Dell City related to the ice storm.  Reports of up to 1 inch radius ice was on powerlines causing these outages.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A winter storm moved into southeast Texas on the night of the 24th. A storm chaser shared a video on social media of sleet falling in Conroe late that night. During the early morning hours of the 25th, the ASOS station at Conroe-North Houston Regional Airport KCXO reported freezing rain. Not long after, a member of the public shared pictures on social media, showing sleet beginning to accumulate in Shenandoah (southern Montgomery County). A NWS Employee also reported that streets and highways in the area were mostly wet during the pre-dawn hours, but some parts of the road had ice glazed over them. This employee also reported around 0.20 inches of sleet. A few hours later, local law enforcement reported ice on I-45 North at SH 242. An emergency manager reported 0.06 inches of ice near Patton Village. In the aftermath of the winter precipitation, Texas department of transportation (TXDOT) reported closures on Woodlands Parkway flyover (Woodlands Parkway and I-45), for both the northbound and southbound lanes.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Across South Texas and the Coastal Bend, persistent dry conditions through late January led to worsening drought and critically low soil moisture, limiting agricultural progress and stressing rangeland. Periods of unseasonably warm weather were followed by hard freezes and a winter storm, though precipitation was generally limited, with only modest rainfall of up to around an inch in parts of the Coastal Bend providing minor short-term improvement to soil moisture. Producers largely completed field preparation but delayed spring planting due to insufficient moisture for germination. Winter pastures and forage growth struggled under the dry conditions, resulting in poor to fair range conditions and increased reliance on hay and supplemental feed for livestock. While citrus and cool-season vegetable harvests continued, drought stress remained a concern for crop development and pasture recovery, and additional rainfall will be needed to improve soil moisture and support the upcoming planting season.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Introduction of D2 drought.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong arctic cold front moved across west Texas and southeast New Mexico during the afternoon and evening hours of the 23rd. Meanwhile, a potent upper-level trough neared the region from the west. Widespread rain began during the morning of the 23rd in western portions of the area and gradually transitioned eastward through the day. As the front moved across the area, rain transitioned to sleet and snow from north to south (with freezing rain being more common south of the Pecos River and in the Davis Mountains). Off and on bands of sleet and snow continued across the Permian Basin and southeast New Mexico on the 24th, and became mostly snow by the 25th before moving east of the area late in the afternoon. Snowfall/sleet totals reached winter storm criteria across much of the northern basin and in southeast New Mexico. Lower snow and ice totals were reported further south.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A member of the public reported a two day sleet/snow total of 3 inches of snow and 1 inch of sleet. The report was received via social media. The total duration of the event is estimated from AWOS data and radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The passage of a very subtle reinforcing front and high pressure settling over the region and gradually progressing eastward through the night, locked in light, variable, but mostly offshore winds for a cool, dry overnight into Sunday morning. This set us up for a chilly night, with light freezes experienced across much of the northern CWA.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: KNQI reported temperatures of 32 degF or less for a least 2 hours.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A prolonged period of winter weather affected South Texas during the final week of January 2026, beginning with the arrival of a strong Arctic front early on January 24. The front surged southward faster than initially anticipated, producing a rapid temperature drop across the region and widespread rain behind the boundary. As colder air deepened overnight, precipitation continued while temperatures approached or fell below freezing across parts of the region, creating a narrow window for freezing rain and drizzle late January 24 into the morning of January 25. The greatest risk for ice accumulation occurred across the Victoria Crossroads, where light ice totals of up to around a tenth of an inch were possible. Elsewhere, the combination of lingering precipitation and wet roadways raised concerns for patchy black ice, particularly on bridges and overpasses as temperatures briefly dipped to freezing.||Once the precipitation ended on January 25, the primary hazard transitioned to extreme cold as a deep Arctic air mass settled over South Texas. Temperatures struggled to rise above the 40s during the day, while overnight lows dropped into the teens across northern inland areas and the lower to mid-20s closer to the coast. Persistent northerly winds produced dangerously low wind chills, with values falling into the single digits in some inland locations and the teens elsewhere. Extreme Cold Warnings and Freeze Warnings were issued across the region as the prolonged cold posed risks to infrastructure, agriculture, and vulnerable populations. Clearer skies and lighter winds early in the week allowed efficient radiational cooling, reinforcing the cold conditions through January 27 before gradual moderation began.||Although temperatures slowly recovered into the 50s and 60s by midweek, the pattern remained active with additional frontal passages. A brief warmup ahead of another cold front late in the week pushed temperatures into the 70s before colder air returned by January 30. This secondary surge brought another round of below-freezing temperatures and widespread cold weather headlines, particularly across inland counties where lows fell into the 20s and wind chills dropped into the teens. While precipitation with this second front remained limited, the extended period of repeated freezes and persistent cold made this late-January event a notable winter episode for South Texas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The AWOS 8T6 in George West / Live Oak reported temperatures of 32 degF or less for a least 2 hours.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The I-35 Corridor, Rio Grande and Coastal Plains received less than normal precipitation during the month, and the drought worsened or remained unchanged. Caldwell, Fayette, Guadalupe, Hays, Lavaca, Maverick, Travis, and Zavala Counties went from Severe (D2) Drought category to Extreme (D3) Drought. Williamson County went from Moderate (D1) Drought to D2. Atascosa, Bastrop, Bexar, Comal, De Witt, Dimmit, Frio, Gonzales, Karnes, Lee, Medina, and Wilson Counties remained in D3. Blanco, Kendall, and Kinney remained in D2. The Edwards Aquifer level was unchanged but was still 39.1 feet below normal. Area reservoirs were below normal conservation levels. Lake Travis dropped 0.5 feet and was 13.8 feet below normal. Canyon Lake dropped 0.6 feet and was 21.0 feet below normal. The 7-day average streamflow was much below (<10%) normal on the Lavaca, Blanco, San Marcos, lower Guadalupe, Medina, lower Nueces, and Atascosa Rivers, and below (10%-24%) normal on the San Gabriel, Colorado, upper Guadalupe, San Antonio, and Frio Rivers. Most water providers encouraged conservation while San Antonio and Universal City imposed stage 3 restrictions and New Braunfels and Austin had stage 2. Of the counties in D2 or worse drought, Atascosa, Bastrop, Blanco, Bexar, Caldwell, Comal, De Witt, Dimmit, Fayette, Frio, Guadalupe, Hays, Karnes, Medina, Wilson, and Zavala had outdoor burn bans in effect at the end of the month.

A winter storm brought ice, sleet and extreme cold to southeast Texas from the 24th through the 26th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A winter storm moved into southeast Texas on the night of the 24th. Broadcast media reported sleet falling in Somerville on the night of the 24th. The next day, broadcast media measured 0.21 inches of ice on a small branch in Frenstat in Burleson County after precipitation had ended.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong arctic cold front moved across west Texas and southeast New Mexico during the afternoon and evening hours of the 23rd. Meanwhile, a potent upper-level trough neared the region from the west. Widespread rain began during the morning of the 23rd in western portions of the area and gradually transitioned eastward through the day. As the front moved across the area, rain transitioned to sleet and snow from north to south (with freezing rain being more common south of the Pecos River and in the Davis Mountains). Off and on bands of sleet and snow continued across the Permian Basin and southeast New Mexico on the 24th, and became mostly snow by the 25th before moving east of the area late in the afternoon. Snowfall/sleet totals reached winter storm criteria across much of the northern basin and in southeast New Mexico. Lower snow and ice totals were reported further south.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A member of the public reported 4.5 inches of storm total snow/sleet. The total duration of the event is estimated from radar and nearby AWOS reports.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from September through December 2025 led to the development of severe (D2) and extreme (D3) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across much of Red River County Texas from the second week of January through the end of the month. During this time, rainfall amounts ranged from 4-7 inches, which was only around 25% of normal, resulting in considerable hardships from area agricultural producers. Pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires was also noted especially as lower humidities to end the year accelerated the drying of fuels. These conditions only accelerated during December as only a tenth up to a half inch of rain fell during the month throughout the county. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well.

A weak cold front extended from Eastern Oklahoma into Northeast Texas during the late evening into the early morning hours of January 9th-10th, and separated a warm, moist, and unstable air mass to its east, with a slightly cooler but drier air mass to the west. A surface low developed during the evening and overnight hours along the frontal boundary, enhancing a deep southerly low level flow into East Texas and North Louisiana, with a longwave trough shifting east through the Rockies into the Southern Plains enhancing large scale forcing along and ahead of the front across the warm sector. Thus, scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms developed across this area, some of which produced locally heavy rainfall in the city of Tyler in Smith County Texas. Localized flash flooding was observed here where high water covered Loop 323 near Troup Highway and University Street, before the storms shifted east into Northwest Louisiana shortly after midnight and produced insolated instances of severe weather.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: High water covered Loop 323 near Troup Highway and University Street in Tyler.

During this time, rainfall amounts ranged from 5-8 inches, which was only 25-30% of normal, resulting in considerable hardships from area agricultural producers. Pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires was also noted especially as lower humidities to end the year accelerated the drying of fuels. Conditions deteriorated to extreme drought across Franklin and Titus Counties by January 22nd through the end of the month as only 1.0-1.5 inches of precipitation fell during the month. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well.

Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with the above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. As a result, extreme (D3) drought had expanded farther southeast from Red River, Franklin, and Titus Counties to start the month into Western Bowie, Morris, and Camp Counties.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper level weather system moved across the High Plains region and brought down very strong winds to the surface from the late morning to the late afternoon on February 17, 2026. A wide array of high winds in the 60 mph range affected the majority of the Texas Panhandle and some locations even experienced wind gusts over 70 mph. Damage to homes, structures, and overturned semi-trucks occurred during the afternoon as a result of these stronger winds. Blowing dust and extreme critical fire weather conditions were also present thanks to the strong winds and several wildfires occurred across the Texas Panhandle as a result.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The peak wind gust in Armstrong County was 60 mph and this was observed at the Goodnight mesonet at 1307CST. Gusts greater than 58 mph were observed in the county from about 1200CST through 1400CST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Lack of rainfall, top five-ten heat, and a flash drought situation with extremely low top-soil moisture levels allowed Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) Drought conditions to worsen as February approached March.  Exceptional (D4) Drought developed on the 17th across the Brush Country - just the fourth small area in the nation at the time (others were in the Texas Big Bend, central Colorado, and northeast Arkansas).  By month's end, the Texas Agrilife Crop and Weather report described soil moisture conditions as extremely poor, with range and pasture forages in poor condition and in some cases, cattle ranchers were liquidating herds. ||Loss/impact reports will be provided for the end of March StormData, when region-wide seasonal drought conditions peaked.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter 2026 led to the continuation of severe (D2) and extreme (D3) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across much of East Texas through the month of February. Rainfall amounts during February only tallied to 0.50-1.75 inches, which was less than half of the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with the above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. As a result, extreme (D3) drought had expanded farther southeast from Red River, Franklin, and Titus Counties to start the month into Western Bowie, Morris, and Camp Counties.

In addition, Xcel Energy implemented a Public Safety Power Shutoff (PSPS) to reduce wildfire risk, which affected thousands of customers and resulted in some schools closing for the day due to lack of electricity and ability to feed students. The cause of the fire is undetermined.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level trough ejected east-northeast from the Desert Southwest into Northwest Texas and Western Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of February 14th, which resulted in the increase of very warm, humid air north across the region from the Gulf. In advance of this system, southwest flow aloft became established, with increasing instability at the surface and aloft coupled with strong wind shear and an approaching cold front enhancing large scale ascent across much of the Four State Region. As a result, showers and thunderstorms, some of which became severe over portions of East Texas and Central Louisiana, developed and spread east across the area during the late afternoon through the evening. Multiple reports of wind damage were received, with a brief, weak isolated tornado having been spawned in Northeast Shelby County near the James community.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree downed along FM Road 757.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper level weather system moved across the High Plains region and brought down very strong winds to the surface from the late morning to the late afternoon on February 17, 2026. A wide array of high winds in the 60 mph range affected the majority of the Texas Panhandle and some locations even experienced wind gusts over 70 mph. Damage to homes, structures, and overturned semi-trucks occurred during the afternoon as a result of these stronger winds. Blowing dust and extreme critical fire weather conditions were also present thanks to the strong winds and several wildfires occurred across the Texas Panhandle as a result.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The 8 Ball Fire ignited on February 17, 2026, approximately 12 miles west of Clarendon, or ten miles west of Howardwick, along the US 287 corridor in Armstrong County. The fire was fueled by freeze-cured tall grasses and brush, driven by critical fire weather conditions including wind gusts up to 45 mph and low humidity. It exhibited rapid growth initially, spreading from a reported 200 acres to thousands of acres within the first 24 hours. Forward progress of the fire was stopped on the evening of February 18th but was contained on February 21st. In total, Eight Ball Fire burned 13563 acres across Armstrong and Donley counties.  There were evacuations in the Howardwick area on February 17th, which were lifted later on February 18th. US Highway 287 was closed from Goodnight to Ashtola for a couple of hours. Highway 70 was also briefly closed. The fire threatened approximately 1,100 homes and critical infrastructure. At the peak of the event, roughly 400 homes were evacuated.  The cause of the fire is unknown.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant winter storm occurred across the southern, eastern, and northeastern United States during January 23-26, 2026. A strong low pressure system moved across Baja California toward the Desert Southwest and then across the southern to northeastern portions of the country during this time frame. This low pressure system was preceded by a strong arctic cold front, which dropped surface temperatures down to record breaking lows across portions of the southern United States, including the Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles. Winter impacts were felt across nearly half of the country, with around an inch of freezing rain occurring at some areas across the southeastern US, inches of sleet across portions of north Texas, and up to one to two feet of snow for the Midwest into New England. This winter storm brought mostly snow to the region, but also there was some sleet mixed in across the southern and southeastern Texas Panhandle during the onset of precipitation across the region. Two to three day snow accumulation across the area ranged from just over an inch across the northwestern Panhandles to around nine to ten inches for the southeast Texas Panhandle. Frigid temperatures were also associated with this system and wind chill values dropped to as low as -20 to -25��F in the early morning hours during this time period. Temperatures remained below freezing across most of the Panhandles from early Friday morning behind the cold front passage until midday on Monday, January 26. The combination of the dangerously cold temperatures and impactful snowfall led to the closure of multiple school districts across the region as well as businesses and local government buildings. A few locations also saw infrastructure impacts such as pipes bursting in the region. Several counties also opened warming centers for the prolonged cold weather.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Spearman and Gruver both received an estimate two inches of snow. Overall the county observed up to two inches.

The highest sleet and snow totals were north of Interstate 20, and the highest freezing rain totals were in our far eastern counties. In addition to the wintry precipitation, bitterly cold air accompanied the system meeting Extreme Cold Warning criteria through the 27th. Unfortunately 8 deaths were reported with this event.

The highest sleet, snow, and freezing rain totals were reported near Paris. Scattered trees and power lines were knocked down due to ice across Lamar County with some roads blocked and power outages, especially from Paris into northeast portions of the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An Arctic cold front ushered in the coldest air mass of the season to Deep South Texas and the Rio Grande Valley with widespread cold temperatures between January 25-27, 2026. Cold temperatures (wind chill) below 30F arrived during the late evening of the 24th across the ranchlands and spread to the lower Rio Grande Valley before daybreak on the 25th.  A cold afternoon set the stage for the overnight of the 25th into the morning of the 26th, as skies cleared but fresh breezes/stronger winds near the coast prevailed.  The 26th was the coldest ambient and feels-like temperature of the calendar year so far, with a freeze in all areas, and wind chill below 20F in most areas.  ||Clear skies and calm winds allowed rapid temperature drops during the evening of the 26th, with many inland locations recording their second hard freeze in as many nights early on the 27th. Locations closer to the coast saw winds veer to the northeast above the surface, precluding a second freeze/hard freeze. ||The hard freeze caused minor damage to tender vegetation and crops in Hidalgo, Willacy, and Cameron County.  Dollar values were unknown as of this writing (end of March 2026) but some estimates are included, and will likely be updated.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Brownsville/South Padre Island International Airport  (BRO) recorded minimum wind chill values at or below 30F degrees (Cold Weather Advisory Criteria) for 6 hours from 4:35-10:20am CST on Sunday January 25th. Harlingen/Valley International Airport (HRL) recorded minimum wind chill values at or below 30F degrees (Cold Weather Advisory Criteria) for 11.5 hours from 11:25pm (Jan 24th) to 10:40am CST January 25th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A prolonged period of winter weather affected South Texas during the final week of January 2026, beginning with the arrival of a strong Arctic front early on January 24. The front surged southward faster than initially anticipated, producing a rapid temperature drop across the region and widespread rain behind the boundary. As colder air deepened overnight, precipitation continued while temperatures approached or fell below freezing across parts of the region, creating a narrow window for freezing rain and drizzle late January 24 into the morning of January 25. The greatest risk for ice accumulation occurred across the Victoria Crossroads, where light ice totals of up to around a tenth of an inch were possible. Elsewhere, the combination of lingering precipitation and wet roadways raised concerns for patchy black ice, particularly on bridges and overpasses as temperatures briefly dipped to freezing.||Once the precipitation ended on January 25, the primary hazard transitioned to extreme cold as a deep Arctic air mass settled over South Texas. Temperatures struggled to rise above the 40s during the day, while overnight lows dropped into the teens across northern inland areas and the lower to mid-20s closer to the coast. Persistent northerly winds produced dangerously low wind chills, with values falling into the single digits in some inland locations and the teens elsewhere. Extreme Cold Warnings and Freeze Warnings were issued across the region as the prolonged cold posed risks to infrastructure, agriculture, and vulnerable populations. Clearer skies and lighter winds early in the week allowed efficient radiational cooling, reinforcing the cold conditions through January 27 before gradual moderation began.||Although temperatures slowly recovered into the 50s and 60s by midweek, the pattern remained active with additional frontal passages. A brief warmup ahead of another cold front late in the week pushed temperatures into the 70s before colder air returned by January 30. This secondary surge brought another round of below-freezing temperatures and widespread cold weather headlines, particularly across inland counties where lows fell into the 20s and wind chills dropped into the teens. While precipitation with this second front remained limited, the extended period of repeated freezes and persistent cold made this late-January event a notable winter episode for South Texas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme Cold/Wind Chill: KVCT reported wind chills at or below 15 degF for at least 2 hours, which is our local Extreme Cold Warning criteria.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An Arctic cold front ushered in the coldest air mass of the season to Deep South Texas and the Rio Grande Valley with widespread cold temperatures between January 25-27, 2026. Cold temperatures (wind chill) below 30F arrived during the late evening of the 24th across the ranchlands and spread to the lower Rio Grande Valley before daybreak on the 25th. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Nearly all of South-Central Texas received less than 50% of normal precipitation during the month, and most counties stayed in the same drought category. The one change was Dimmit County which went from Extreme (D3) Drought to Exceptional (D4) Drought. Atascosa, Bastrop, Bexar, Caldwell, Comal, De Witt, Fayette, Frio, Gonzales, Guadalupe, Hays, Karnes, Lavaca, Lee, Maverick, Medina, Travis, Wilson, and Zavala Counties stayed in D3. Blanco, Kendall, Kinney, and Williamson stayed in Severe (D2) Drought. The Edwards Aquifer level dropped 2.0 feet and was 41.0 feet below normal. Area reservoirs were below normal conservation levels. Lake Travis dropped 1.4 feet and was 15.2 feet below normal. Canyon Lake dropped 0.5 feet and was 21.5 feet below normal. The 7-day average streamflow was much below (<10%) normal on the Lavaca, Blanco, San Marcos, lower Guadalupe, Medina, and Atascosa Rivers, and below (10%-24%) normal on the San Gabriel, Colorado, San Antonio, lower Nueces, and Frio Rivers. Most water providers encouraged conservation while San Antonio and Universal City imposed stage 3 restrictions and New Braunfels and Austin had stage 2.  Of the counties in D2 or worse drought, Atascosa, Bastrop, Blanco, Bexar, Caldwell, Comal, De Witt, Dimmit, Fayette, Frio, Gonzales, Guadalupe, Hays, Karnes, Lee, Medina, Travis, Williamson, Wilson, and Zavala had outdoor burn bans in effect at the end of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Across South Texas and the Coastal Bend during February, persistent drought and very limited rainfall continued to strain agricultural conditions. Periods of freezing temperatures early in the month caused damage to several leafy vegetable crops and burned back pasture grasses, while most areas received little meaningful precipitation despite occasional scattered showers. Soil moisture remained very short across much of the region, with some irrigation canals and stock tanks running low or dry. These dry conditions delayed widespread planting of corn, sorghum, and other row crops, as many producers waited for sufficient soil moisture to support germination, though limited planting began where moisture allowed. Irrigated small grains such as oats and wheat generally held up better than dryland fields, and onion harvest began with strong yields despite earlier cold stress. Rangeland and pasture conditions remained poor to very poor, forcing livestock producers to rely heavily on hay and supplemental feed as supplies tightened and forage availability declined. As drought impacts persisted, some producers reduced herd sizes, though strong cattle markets continued to provide some financial support.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Continued D2 and D3 drought. Introduction of D4 on 2/24.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An Arctic cold front ushered in the coldest air mass of the season to Deep South Texas and the Rio Grande Valley with widespread cold temperatures between January 25-27, 2026. Cold temperatures (wind chill) below 30F arrived during the late evening of the 24th across the ranchlands and spread to the lower Rio Grande Valley before daybreak on the 25th.  A cold afternoon set the stage for the overnight of the 25th into the morning of the 26th, as skies cleared but fresh breezes/stronger winds near the coast prevailed.  The 26th was the coldest ambient and feels-like temperature of the calendar year so far, with a freeze in all areas, and wind chill below 20F in most areas.  ||Clear skies and calm winds allowed rapid temperature drops during the evening of the 26th, with many inland locations recording their second hard freeze in as many nights early on the 27th. Locations closer to the coast saw winds veer to the northeast above the surface, precluding a second freeze/hard freeze. ||The hard freeze caused minor damage to tender vegetation and crops in Hidalgo, Willacy, and Cameron County.  Dollar values were unknown as of this writing (end of March 2026) but some estimates are included, and will likely be updated.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hebbronville recorded minimum wind chill values at or below 25F degrees (Cold Weather Advisory Criteria) for 8.5 hours from 3:15-11:35am CST on the morning of Sunday January 25th.  Minimum temperatures were in the lower 20s.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At the start of the new year, Severe (D2) Drought was sited across much of the Northern Ranchlands and the Upper valley including the Northwestern section of Kenedy County, southeastern Brooks, northwestern Jim Hogg, eastern Zapata, and much of Starr County. Meanwhile, Extreme (D3) Drought was over much of Brooks and Jim Hogg counties, northwestern Starr county, and extreme northwestern Kenedy County at the start of the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, D2 Severe Drought to D3 Extreme Drought was seen over Brooks County at the start of the month of January, with D3 Drought encompassing the northwestern half of the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broken line of thunderstorms associated with an upper trough and Pacific cold front pushed through North and Central Texas on February 14. Storms were mostly below severe thresholds, but a few became strong enough to produce wind damage and isolated instances of flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Videos and articles from social and news media reported that a wind turbine south of Caddo was struck by lightning the morning of February 14th and caught on fire as a result. As per pictures, the shell at the top of the turbine was destroyed along with one of the blades.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An approaching upper-level trough interacted with anomalously high moisture across west Texas, resulting in shower and thunderstorm development that afternoon and evening. Initially isolated to scattered showers and storms eventually intensified and coalesced into a broken line as they moved across the Permian Basin. Large hail was reported near Monahans before the line developed. Heavy rain also led to flash flooding in the Midland/Odessa area. Additional convection developed later that night, but no additional severe reports were received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An off-duty NWS Employee reported street flooding in the Gardendale area. The total time of occurrence is partially estimated by radar. No damage was reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm chances increased across South Texas on February 14th as a large-scale upper-level trough moved east from the western United States and pushed an associated surface low and cold front toward the region. Ahead of the front, a strengthening low-level jet transported Gulf moisture northward, gradually increasing atmospheric moisture and supporting scattered showers overnight into the morning hours. Early activity remained relatively light and limited in coverage, primarily affecting the Coastal Bend, Victoria Crossroads, and northern Brush Country as modest lift interacted with increasing low-level moisture.||By the afternoon and evening, the approaching cold front provided stronger lift across the region while upper-level jet support enhanced large-scale ascent. Atmospheric moisture values rose to well above seasonal normals, and modest instability developed with CAPE values near 1000 J/kg. These ingredients allowed showers and thunderstorms to develop along and ahead of the advancing boundary, with the greatest coverage focused across northern portions of the area where mid-level capping was weakest. Storms were expected to organize into a broken line as they moved from northwest to southeast through the afternoon and evening.||Although the overall severe weather risk remained limited, portions of the northern Brush Country, northern Coastal Plains, and Victoria Crossroads were placed under a Marginal Risk (level 1 of 5) for severe thunderstorms. South Texas largely remained on the southwestern edge of the more favorable severe environment centered farther north and east across Southeast Texas. However, a few storms briefly intensified as the front moved through, producing isolated damaging wind gusts, and severe hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet station FW9607 Kingsville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front brought in freezing temperatures to the Northern Ranchlands from northern Jim Hogg to Kenedy County on January 18-19. The front followed a prolonged stretch of unseasonably warm weather through the 9th, then a period of near-average conditions from the 10th-17th. On January 19th, the combination of the cold airmass and strong radiational cooling resulted in freezing temperatures.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hebbronville recorded freezing temperatures (32F degrees or lower) for 2 hours from 5:35-7:35am CST on January 18th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An Arctic cold front ushered in the coldest air mass of the season to Deep South Texas and the Rio Grande Valley with widespread cold temperatures between January 25-27, 2026. Cold temperatures (wind chill) below 30F arrived during the late evening of the 24th across the ranchlands and spread to the lower Rio Grande Valley before daybreak on the 25th.  A cold afternoon set the stage for the overnight of the 25th into the morning of the 26th, as skies cleared but fresh breezes/stronger winds near the coast prevailed.  The 26th was the coldest ambient and feels-like temperature of the calendar year so far, with a freeze in all areas, and wind chill below 20F in most areas.  ||Clear skies and calm winds allowed rapid temperature drops during the evening of the 26th, with many inland locations recording their second hard freeze in as many nights early on the 27th. Locations closer to the coast saw winds veer to the northeast above the surface, precluding a second freeze/hard freeze. ||The hard freeze caused minor damage to tender vegetation and crops in Hidalgo, Willacy, and Cameron County.  Dollar values were unknown as of this writing (end of March 2026) but some estimates are included, and will likely be updated.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Port Isabel Airport (PIL) recorded minimum wind chill values at or below 30F degrees (Cold Weather Advisory Criteria) for 9 hours from 2:00-10:50am CST on Sunday January 25th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An approaching upper-level trough interacted with anomalously high moisture across west Texas, resulting in shower and thunderstorm development that afternoon and evening. Initially isolated to scattered showers and storms eventually intensified and coalesced into a broken line as they moved across the Permian Basin. Large hail was reported near Monahans before the line developed. Heavy rain also led to flash flooding in the Midland/Odessa area. Additional convection developed later that night, but no additional severe reports were received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An mPING report of street flooding in Midland was received from the public. No additional details were provided, and no damages were reported. The total time of occurrence is partially estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant winter storm occurred across the southern, eastern, and northeastern United States during January 23-26, 2026. A strong low pressure system moved across Baja California toward the Desert Southwest and then across the southern to northeastern portions of the country during this time frame. This low pressure system was preceded by a strong arctic cold front, which dropped surface temperatures down to record breaking lows across portions of the southern United States, including the Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles. Winter impacts were felt across nearly half of the country, with around an inch of freezing rain occurring at some areas across the southeastern US, inches of sleet across portions of north Texas, and up to one to two feet of snow for the Midwest into New England. This winter storm brought mostly snow to the region, but also there was some sleet mixed in across the southern and southeastern Texas Panhandle during the onset of precipitation across the region. Two to three day snow accumulation across the area ranged from just over an inch across the northwestern Panhandles to around nine to ten inches for the southeast Texas Panhandle. Frigid temperatures were also associated with this system and wind chill values dropped to as low as -20 to -25��F in the early morning hours during this time period. Temperatures remained below freezing across most of the Panhandles from early Friday morning behind the cold front passage until midday on Monday, January 26. The combination of the dangerously cold temperatures and impactful snowfall led to the closure of multiple school districts across the region as well as businesses and local government buildings. A few locations also saw infrastructure impacts such as pipes bursting in the region. Several counties also opened warming centers for the prolonged cold weather.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A sharp gradient of snow occurred from northwest to southeast across the county. The lowest snowfall amounts of around one to two inches occurred in the northwest while amounts around three inches occurred in the southeast. Stinnett measured one inch of snow, 1.6 inches was measured just west of Fritch and around 2.9 to 3 inches of snow occurred around Borger.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant winter storm occurred across the southern, eastern, and northeastern United States during January 23-26, 2026. A strong low pressure system moved across Baja California toward the Desert Southwest and then across the southern to northeastern portions of the country during this time frame. This low pressure system was preceded by a strong arctic cold front, which dropped surface temperatures down to record breaking lows across portions of the southern United States, including the Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles. Winter impacts were felt across nearly half of the country, with around an inch of freezing rain occurring at some areas across the southeastern US, inches of sleet across portions of north Texas, and up to one to two feet of snow for the Midwest into New England. This winter storm brought mostly snow to the region, but also there was some sleet mixed in across the southern and southeastern Texas Panhandle during the onset of precipitation across the region. Two to three day snow accumulation across the area ranged from just over an inch across the northwestern Panhandles to around nine to ten inches for the southeast Texas Panhandle. Frigid temperatures were also associated with this system and wind chill values dropped to as low as -20 to -25��F in the early morning hours during this time period. Temperatures remained below freezing across most of the Panhandles from early Friday morning behind the cold front passage until midday on Monday, January 26. The combination of the dangerously cold temperatures and impactful snowfall led to the closure of multiple school districts across the region as well as businesses and local government buildings. A few locations also saw infrastructure impacts such as pipes bursting in the region. Several counties also opened warming centers for the prolonged cold weather.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This system dropped 2 to 4 of snow in the northern two thirds of the county from Canyon to Amarillo. While it is possible there was up to 5 inches in the south, closest to the heavier swath of snow, there were no measurements confirmed. 2.4 to 3 inches of snow fell around Canyon and Palo Duro Canyon. The south and southwest side of Amarillo measured 2 to 3 inches.

The highest sleet and snow totals were north of Interstate 20, and the highest freezing rain totals were in our far eastern counties. In addition to the wintry precipitation, bitterly cold air accompanied the system meeting Extreme Cold Warning criteria through the 27th. Unfortunately 8 deaths were reported with this event.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Across South Texas and the Coastal Bend, persistent dry conditions through late January led to worsening drought and critically low soil moisture, limiting agricultural progress and stressing rangeland. Periods of unseasonably warm weather were followed by hard freezes and a winter storm, though precipitation was generally limited, with only modest rainfall of up to around an inch in parts of the Coastal Bend providing minor short-term improvement to soil moisture. Producers largely completed field preparation but delayed spring planting due to insufficient moisture for germination. Winter pastures and forage growth struggled under the dry conditions, resulting in poor to fair range conditions and increased reliance on hay and supplemental feed for livestock. While citrus and cool-season vegetable harvests continued, drought stress remained a concern for crop development and pasture recovery, and additional rainfall will be needed to improve soil moisture and support the upcoming planting season.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Continued D2 drought.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: KBEA reported temperatures of 32 degF or less for a least 2 hours.

The highest sleet and snow totals were north of Interstate 20, and the highest freezing rain totals were in our far eastern counties. In addition to the wintry precipitation, bitterly cold air accompanied the system meeting Extreme Cold Warning criteria through the 27th. Unfortunately 8 deaths were reported with this event.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An Arctic cold front ushered in the coldest air mass of the season to Deep South Texas and the Rio Grande Valley with widespread cold temperatures between January 25-27, 2026. Cold temperatures (wind chill) below 30F arrived during the late evening of the 24th across the ranchlands and spread to the lower Rio Grande Valley before daybreak on the 25th.  A cold afternoon set the stage for the overnight of the 25th into the morning of the 26th, as skies cleared but fresh breezes/stronger winds near the coast prevailed. Rincon del San Jose (southeast Kenedy) reached 27F by midnight; interpolating between the sites indicated that Willacy Island reached 30F around or just after midnight on the 25th.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme Cold Warning Criteria (Wind chills at or below 15F) was reached Baffin Bay (Texas Coastal Ocean Observation Network, TCOON) at around 5 AM, continuing through 9 AM.  Values bottomed out at 13F around 9 AM at the site, on the Kenedy/Kleberg County line.  Slightly lower durations were noted at TCOON Rincon del San Jose (6 to 9 AM). EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A compact but strong upper level short wave trough tracked across Baja California on the afternoon of the 13th. Large scale ascent from an upper level jet streak interacted with abundant moisture streaming overhead at mid and upper levels of the atmosphere. Low level moisture streaming into the region combined with warm surface temperatures creating an unstable atmosphere by late afternoon. This resulted in scattered thunderstorms from late in the afternoon through the evening hours of the 13th. One of these storms produced severe winds near Slaton (Lubbock County). The abundant amount of moisture in the atmosphere also was able to produce heavy rainfall and flash flooding within the city of Lubbock (Lubbock County). Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet sites measured rainfall rates as high as four inches per hour.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Slaton measured severe wind gusts from 1947 CST through 1950 CST. A peak wind gust of 65 mph was measured at 1947 CST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful upper level storm system that spread eastward from the Intermountain West brought widespread high winds, blowing dust, and a few wildfires on the morning and afternoon of the 17th. Thick high level cloud cover early in the day initially prevented strong winds from developing. However, these clouds began to thin out and clear by late in the morning from west to east. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Across South Texas and the Coastal Bend during February, persistent drought and very limited rainfall continued to strain agricultural conditions. Periods of freezing temperatures early in the month caused damage to several leafy vegetable crops and burned back pasture grasses, while most areas received little meaningful precipitation despite occasional scattered showers. Soil moisture remained very short across much of the region, with some irrigation canals and stock tanks running low or dry. These dry conditions delayed widespread planting of corn, sorghum, and other row crops, as many producers waited for sufficient soil moisture to support germination, though limited planting began where moisture allowed. Irrigated small grains such as oats and wheat generally held up better than dryland fields, and onion harvest began with strong yields despite earlier cold stress. Rangeland and pasture conditions remained poor to very poor, forcing livestock producers to rely heavily on hay and supplemental feed as supplies tightened and forage availability declined. As drought impacts persisted, some producers reduced herd sizes, though strong cattle markets continued to provide some financial support.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Continued D2 drought.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Across South Texas and the Coastal Bend during February, persistent drought and very limited rainfall continued to strain agricultural conditions. Periods of freezing temperatures early in the month caused damage to several leafy vegetable crops and burned back pasture grasses, while most areas received little meaningful precipitation despite occasional scattered showers. Soil moisture remained very short across much of the region, with some irrigation canals and stock tanks running low or dry. These dry conditions delayed widespread planting of corn, sorghum, and other row crops, as many producers waited for sufficient soil moisture to support germination, though limited planting began where moisture allowed. Irrigated small grains such as oats and wheat generally held up better than dryland fields, and onion harvest began with strong yields despite earlier cold stress. Rangeland and pasture conditions remained poor to very poor, forcing livestock producers to rely heavily on hay and supplemental feed as supplies tightened and forage availability declined. As drought impacts persisted, some producers reduced herd sizes, though strong cattle markets continued to provide some financial support.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Continued D2 and D3 drought.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm chances increased across South Texas on February 14th as a large-scale upper-level trough moved east from the western United States and pushed an associated surface low and cold front toward the region. Ahead of the front, a strengthening low-level jet transported Gulf moisture northward, gradually increasing atmospheric moisture and supporting scattered showers overnight into the morning hours. Early activity remained relatively light and limited in coverage, primarily affecting the Coastal Bend, Victoria Crossroads, and northern Brush Country as modest lift interacted with increasing low-level moisture.||By the afternoon and evening, the approaching cold front provided stronger lift across the region while upper-level jet support enhanced large-scale ascent. Atmospheric moisture values rose to well above seasonal normals, and modest instability developed with CAPE values near 1000 J/kg. These ingredients allowed showers and thunderstorms to develop along and ahead of the advancing boundary, with the greatest coverage focused across northern portions of the area where mid-level capping was weakest. Storms were expected to organize into a broken line as they moved from northwest to southeast through the afternoon and evening.||Although the overall severe weather risk remained limited, portions of the northern Brush Country, northern Coastal Plains, and Victoria Crossroads were placed under a Marginal Risk (level 1 of 5) for severe thunderstorms. South Texas largely remained on the southwestern edge of the more favorable severe environment centered farther north and east across Southeast Texas. However, a few storms briefly intensified as the front moved through, producing isolated damaging wind gusts, and severe hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report from mPING: Half Dollar (1.25 in.).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Nearly all of South-Central Texas received less than 50% of normal precipitation during the month, and most counties stayed in the same drought category. The one change was Dimmit County which went from Extreme (D3) Drought to Exceptional (D4) Drought. Atascosa, Bastrop, Bexar, Caldwell, Comal, De Witt, Fayette, Frio, Gonzales, Guadalupe, Hays, Karnes, Lavaca, Lee, Maverick, Medina, Travis, Wilson, and Zavala Counties stayed in D3. Blanco, Kendall, Kinney, and Williamson stayed in Severe (D2) Drought. The Edwards Aquifer level dropped 2.0 feet and was 41.0 feet below normal. Area reservoirs were below normal conservation levels. Lake Travis dropped 1.4 feet and was 15.2 feet below normal. Canyon Lake dropped 0.5 feet and was 21.5 feet below normal. The 7-day average streamflow was much below (<10%) normal on the Lavaca, Blanco, San Marcos, lower Guadalupe, Medina, and Atascosa Rivers, and below (10%-24%) normal on the San Gabriel, Colorado, San Antonio, lower Nueces, and Frio Rivers. Most water providers encouraged conservation while San Antonio and Universal City imposed stage 3 restrictions and New Braunfels and Austin had stage 2.  Of the counties in D2 or worse drought, Atascosa, Bastrop, Blanco, Bexar, Caldwell, Comal, De Witt, Dimmit, Fayette, Frio, Gonzales, Guadalupe, Hays, Karnes, Lee, Medina, Travis, Williamson, Wilson, and Zavala had outdoor burn bans in effect at the end of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A prolonged period of winter weather affected South Texas during the final week of January 2026, beginning with the arrival of a strong Arctic front early on January 24. The front surged southward faster than initially anticipated, producing a rapid temperature drop across the region and widespread rain behind the boundary. As colder air deepened overnight, precipitation continued while temperatures approached or fell below freezing across parts of the region, creating a narrow window for freezing rain and drizzle late January 24 into the morning of January 25. The greatest risk for ice accumulation occurred across the Victoria Crossroads, where light ice totals of up to around a tenth of an inch were possible. Elsewhere, the combination of lingering precipitation and wet roadways raised concerns for patchy black ice, particularly on bridges and overpasses as temperatures briefly dipped to freezing.||Once the precipitation ended on January 25, the primary hazard transitioned to extreme cold as a deep Arctic air mass settled over South Texas. Temperatures struggled to rise above the 40s during the day, while overnight lows dropped into the teens across northern inland areas and the lower to mid-20s closer to the coast. Persistent northerly winds produced dangerously low wind chills, with values falling into the single digits in some inland locations and the teens elsewhere. Extreme Cold Warnings and Freeze Warnings were issued across the region as the prolonged cold posed risks to infrastructure, agriculture, and vulnerable populations. Clearer skies and lighter winds early in the week allowed efficient radiational cooling, reinforcing the cold conditions through January 27 before gradual moderation began.||Although temperatures slowly recovered into the 50s and 60s by midweek, the pattern remained active with additional frontal passages. A brief warmup ahead of another cold front late in the week pushed temperatures into the 70s before colder air returned by January 30. This secondary surge brought another round of below-freezing temperatures and widespread cold weather headlines, particularly across inland counties where lows fell into the 20s and wind chills dropped into the teens. While precipitation with this second front remained limited, the extended period of repeated freezes and persistent cold made this late-January event a notable winter episode for South Texas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: KVCT reported wind chills at or below 25 degF for at least 2 hours, which is our local Cold Weather Advisory criteria.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant winter storm occurred across the southern, eastern, and northeastern United States during January 23-26, 2026. A strong low pressure system moved across Baja California toward the Desert Southwest and then across the southern to northeastern portions of the country during this time frame. This low pressure system was preceded by a strong arctic cold front, which dropped surface temperatures down to record breaking lows across portions of the southern United States, including the Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles. Winter impacts were felt across nearly half of the country, with around an inch of freezing rain occurring at some areas across the southeastern US, inches of sleet across portions of north Texas, and up to one to two feet of snow for the Midwest into New England. Two to three day snow accumulation across the area ranged from just over an inch across the northwestern Panhandles to around nine to ten inches for the southeast Texas Panhandle. Temperatures remained below freezing across most of the Panhandles from early Friday morning behind the cold front passage until midday on Monday, January 26. A few locations also saw infrastructure impacts such as pipes bursting in the region. Several counties also opened warming centers for the prolonged cold weather.

Clarendon measured 9.5 to 10.2 inches, Howardwick measured 9 inches, 7 miles east-northeast of Hedley estimated 7 inches of snow and 8 inches of snow occurred two miles south-southeast of Greenbelt Lake. Some sleet occurred during the onset of precipitation on the afternoon and early evening of January 24th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Nearly all of South-Central Texas received less than 50% of normal precipitation during the month, and most counties stayed in the same drought category. The one change was Dimmit County which went from Extreme (D3) Drought to Exceptional (D4) Drought. Atascosa, Bastrop, Bexar, Caldwell, Comal, De Witt, Fayette, Frio, Gonzales, Guadalupe, Hays, Karnes, Lavaca, Lee, Maverick, Medina, Travis, Wilson, and Zavala Counties stayed in D3. Blanco, Kendall, Kinney, and Williamson stayed in Severe (D2) Drought. The Edwards Aquifer level dropped 2.0 feet and was 41.0 feet below normal. Area reservoirs were below normal conservation levels. Lake Travis dropped 1.4 feet and was 15.2 feet below normal. Canyon Lake dropped 0.5 feet and was 21.5 feet below normal. The 7-day average streamflow was much below (<10%) normal on the Lavaca, Blanco, San Marcos, lower Guadalupe, Medina, and Atascosa Rivers, and below (10%-24%) normal on the San Gabriel, Colorado, San Antonio, lower Nueces, and Frio Rivers. Most water providers encouraged conservation while San Antonio and Universal City imposed stage 3 restrictions and New Braunfels and Austin had stage 2.  Of the counties in D2 or worse drought, Atascosa, Bastrop, Blanco, Bexar, Caldwell, Comal, De Witt, Dimmit, Fayette, Frio, Gonzales, Guadalupe, Hays, Karnes, Lee, Medina, Travis, Williamson, Wilson, and Zavala had outdoor burn bans in effect at the end of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Across South Texas and the Coastal Bend during February, persistent drought and very limited rainfall continued to strain agricultural conditions. Periods of freezing temperatures early in the month caused damage to several leafy vegetable crops and burned back pasture grasses, while most areas received little meaningful precipitation despite occasional scattered showers. Soil moisture remained very short across much of the region, with some irrigation canals and stock tanks running low or dry. These dry conditions delayed widespread planting of corn, sorghum, and other row crops, as many producers waited for sufficient soil moisture to support germination, though limited planting began where moisture allowed. Irrigated small grains such as oats and wheat generally held up better than dryland fields, and onion harvest began with strong yields despite earlier cold stress. Rangeland and pasture conditions remained poor to very poor, forcing livestock producers to rely heavily on hay and supplemental feed as supplies tightened and forage availability declined. As drought impacts persisted, some producers reduced herd sizes, though strong cattle markets continued to provide some financial support.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Continued D3 drought. Introduction of D4 on 2/24.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An impactful and long-duration winter storm impacted Oklahoma and western-north Texas beginning on the evening of the 23rd and lasting into the morning of the 25th. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant winter storm occurred across the southern, eastern, and northeastern United States during January 23-26, 2026. A strong low pressure system moved across Baja California toward the Desert Southwest and then across the southern to northeastern portions of the country during this time frame. This low pressure system was preceded by a strong arctic cold front, which dropped surface temperatures down to record breaking lows across portions of the southern United States, including the Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles. Winter impacts were felt across nearly half of the country, with around an inch of freezing rain occurring at some areas across the southeastern US, inches of sleet across portions of north Texas, and up to one to two feet of snow for the Midwest into New England. This winter storm brought mostly snow to the region, but also there was some sleet mixed in across the southern and southeastern Texas Panhandle during the onset of precipitation across the region. Two to three day snow accumulation across the area ranged from just over an inch across the northwestern Panhandles to around nine to ten inches for the southeast Texas Panhandle. Frigid temperatures were also associated with this system and wind chill values dropped to as low as -20 to -25��F in the early morning hours during this time period. Temperatures remained below freezing across most of the Panhandles from early Friday morning behind the cold front passage until midday on Monday, January 26. The combination of the dangerously cold temperatures and impactful snowfall led to the closure of multiple school districts across the region as well as businesses and local government buildings. A few locations also saw infrastructure impacts such as pipes bursting in the region. Several counties also opened warming centers for the prolonged cold weather.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This area was under the heaviest swath of snow that primarily fell during the afternoon of January 24th into the early morning hours of January 25th. The central to northern parts of the county received 8 to 11 inches of snow. 6.5 inches of snow was measured in Wellington. Some sleet occurred during the onset of precipitation during the afternoon and evening hours of January 24th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The only winter weather event of the season occurred January 23-25. A mix of sleet and snow fell across the region, but sleet was the predominant precipitation type. The highest sleet and snow totals were north of Interstate 20, and the highest freezing rain totals were in our far eastern counties. In addition to the wintry precipitation, bitterly cold air accompanied the system meeting Extreme Cold Warning criteria through the 27th. Unfortunately 8 deaths were reported with this event.

The highest sleet and snow totals were north of Interstate 20, and the highest freezing rain totals were in our far eastern counties. In addition to the wintry precipitation, bitterly cold air accompanied the system meeting Extreme Cold Warning criteria through the 27th. Unfortunately 8 deaths were reported with this event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind chills dropped below 5 degrees across the county between Saturday evening and Tuesday morning, January 24th through 27th. The lowest wind chill of 3 was recorded at KT35 the morning of January 25th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Nearly all of South-Central Texas received less than 50% of normal precipitation during the month, and most counties stayed in the same drought category. The one change was Dimmit County which went from Extreme (D3) Drought to Exceptional (D4) Drought. Atascosa, Bastrop, Bexar, Caldwell, Comal, De Witt, Fayette, Frio, Gonzales, Guadalupe, Hays, Karnes, Lavaca, Lee, Maverick, Medina, Travis, Wilson, and Zavala Counties stayed in D3. Blanco, Kendall, Kinney, and Williamson stayed in Severe (D2) Drought. The Edwards Aquifer level dropped 2.0 feet and was 41.0 feet below normal. Area reservoirs were below normal conservation levels. Lake Travis dropped 1.4 feet and was 15.2 feet below normal. Canyon Lake dropped 0.5 feet and was 21.5 feet below normal. The 7-day average streamflow was much below (<10%) normal on the Lavaca, Blanco, San Marcos, lower Guadalupe, Medina, and Atascosa Rivers, and below (10%-24%) normal on the San Gabriel, Colorado, San Antonio, lower Nueces, and Frio Rivers. Most water providers encouraged conservation while San Antonio and Universal City imposed stage 3 restrictions and New Braunfels and Austin had stage 2.  Of the counties in D2 or worse drought, Atascosa, Bastrop, Blanco, Bexar, Caldwell, Comal, De Witt, Dimmit, Fayette, Frio, Gonzales, Guadalupe, Hays, Karnes, Lee, Medina, Travis, Williamson, Wilson, and Zavala had outdoor burn bans in effect at the end of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Across South Texas and the Coastal Bend during February, persistent drought and very limited rainfall continued to strain agricultural conditions. Periods of freezing temperatures early in the month caused damage to several leafy vegetable crops and burned back pasture grasses, while most areas received little meaningful precipitation despite occasional scattered showers. Soil moisture remained very short across much of the region, with some irrigation canals and stock tanks running low or dry. These dry conditions delayed widespread planting of corn, sorghum, and other row crops, as many producers waited for sufficient soil moisture to support germination, though limited planting began where moisture allowed. Irrigated small grains such as oats and wheat generally held up better than dryland fields, and onion harvest began with strong yields despite earlier cold stress. Rangeland and pasture conditions remained poor to very poor, forcing livestock producers to rely heavily on hay and supplemental feed as supplies tightened and forage availability declined. As drought impacts persisted, some producers reduced herd sizes, though strong cattle markets continued to provide some financial support.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Continued D2 and D3 drought. D3 expanded to cover whole county on 2/24.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful upper level storm system that spread eastward from the Intermountain West brought widespread high winds, blowing dust, and a few wildfires on the morning and afternoon of the 17th. Thick high level cloud cover early in the day initially prevented strong winds from developing. However, these clouds began to thin out and clear by late in the morning from west to east. This allowed surface winds to quickly ramp up where clearing occurred. Most observed severe wind gusts were between 58 and 65 mph, however, the Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Olton measured a wind gust of 77 mph. These strong winds also lofted copious amounts of dust into the atmosphere which reduced visibility across the South Plains and extreme southern Texas Panhandle. Observed visibilities dropped as low as one half mile at times. The strong winds and dry conditions also brought favorable wildfire conditions. Several wildfires started across the region with one igniting near Plainview known as the Arbor fire. A prolonged period of winter weather affected South Texas during the final week of January 2026, beginning with the arrival of a strong Arctic front early on January 24. The front surged southward faster than initially anticipated, producing a rapid temperature drop across the region and widespread rain behind the boundary. As colder air deepened overnight, precipitation continued while temperatures approached or fell below freezing across parts of the region, creating a narrow window for freezing rain and drizzle late January 24 into the morning of January 25. The greatest risk for ice accumulation occurred across the Victoria Crossroads, where light ice totals of up to around a tenth of an inch were possible. Elsewhere, the combination of lingering precipitation and wet roadways raised concerns for patchy black ice, particularly on bridges and overpasses as temperatures briefly dipped to freezing.||Once the precipitation ended on January 25, the primary hazard transitioned to extreme cold as a deep Arctic air mass settled over South Texas. Temperatures struggled to rise above the 40s during the day, while overnight lows dropped into the teens across northern inland areas and the lower to mid-20s closer to the coast. Persistent northerly winds produced dangerously low wind chills, with values falling into the single digits in some inland locations and the teens elsewhere. Extreme Cold Warnings and Freeze Warnings were issued across the region as the prolonged cold posed risks to infrastructure, agriculture, and vulnerable populations. Clearer skies and lighter winds early in the week allowed efficient radiational cooling, reinforcing the cold conditions through January 27 before gradual moderation began.||Although temperatures slowly recovered into the 50s and 60s by midweek, the pattern remained active with additional frontal passages. A brief warmup ahead of another cold front late in the week pushed temperatures into the 70s before colder air returned by January 30. This secondary surge brought another round of below-freezing temperatures and widespread cold weather headlines, particularly across inland counties where lows fell into the 20s and wind chills dropped into the teens. While precipitation with this second front remained limited, the extended period of repeated freezes and persistent cold made this late-January event a notable winter episode for South Texas.

As colder air deepened overnight, precipitation continued while temperatures approached or fell below freezing across parts of the region, creating a narrow window for freezing rain and drizzle late January 24 into the morning of January 25. The greatest risk for ice accumulation occurred across the Victoria Crossroads, where light ice totals of up to around a tenth of an inch were possible. Elsewhere, the combination of lingering precipitation and wet roadways raised concerns for patchy black ice, particularly on bridges and overpasses as temperatures briefly dipped to freezing.||Once the precipitation ended on January 25, the primary hazard transitioned to extreme cold as a deep Arctic air mass settled over South Texas. Temperatures struggled to rise above the 40s during the day, while overnight lows dropped into the teens across northern inland areas and the lower to mid-20s closer to the coast. Persistent northerly winds produced dangerously low wind chills, with values falling into the single digits in some inland locations and the teens elsewhere. Extreme Cold Warnings and Freeze Warnings were issued across the region as the prolonged cold posed risks to infrastructure, agriculture, and vulnerable populations. Clearer skies and lighter winds early in the week allowed efficient radiational cooling, reinforcing the cold conditions through January 27 before gradual moderation began.||Although temperatures slowly recovered into the 50s and 60s by midweek, the pattern remained active with additional frontal passages. A brief warmup ahead of another cold front late in the week pushed temperatures into the 70s before colder air returned by January 30. This secondary surge brought another round of below-freezing temperatures and widespread cold weather headlines, particularly across inland counties where lows fell into the 20s and wind chills dropped into the teens. While precipitation with this second front remained limited, the extended period of repeated freezes and persistent cold made this late-January event a notable winter episode for South Texas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: KLRD reported temperatures of 32 degF or less for a least 2 hours.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An impactful and long-duration winter storm impacted Oklahoma and western-north Texas beginning on the evening of the 23rd and lasting into the morning of the 25th. A strong surface high, with origins across far northern latitudes, ushered in a very cold/sub-freezing airmass across the region by the morning of the 23rd. Over the coming 36 hours, increasingly strong west-southwesterly flow (and associated lift) fostered multiple waves of frozen precipitation across the forecast area. Initially, a mix of snow and sleet occurred, owing to a notable warm layer (i.e., warm nose) located between 700 and 800 mb. Eventually, by Saturday evening, continued mid-level cooling allowed for a transition to mostly snow with continued precipitation into Sunday morning.||While individual event narratives are not included for Clay County, with no direct surface observations reported during the event, at least 2 inches of snow/sleet accumulations and slick roadways likely occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The county received a combination of mainly sleet and some snow during this event, producing 1 to 3 inches of accumulation. The highest observed total (3 inches) was reported near Lake Kemp. Listed amounts reflect a synthesis of both remote sensing and direct observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant winter storm occurred across the southern, eastern, and northeastern United States during January 23-26, 2026. A strong low pressure system moved across Baja California toward the Desert Southwest and then across the southern to northeastern portions of the country during this time frame. This low pressure system was preceded by a strong arctic cold front, which dropped surface temperatures down to record breaking lows across portions of the southern United States, including the Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles. Winter impacts were felt across nearly half of the country, with around an inch of freezing rain occurring at some areas across the southeastern US, inches of sleet across portions of north Texas, and up to one to two feet of snow for the Midwest into New England. This winter storm brought mostly snow to the region, but also there was some sleet mixed in across the southern and southeastern Texas Panhandle during the onset of precipitation across the region. Two to three day snow accumulation across the area ranged from just over an inch across the northwestern Panhandles to around nine to ten inches for the southeast Texas Panhandle. Frigid temperatures were also associated with this system and wind chill values dropped to as low as -20 to -25��F in the early morning hours during this time period. Temperatures remained below freezing across most of the Panhandles from early Friday morning behind the cold front passage until midday on Monday, January 26. The combination of the dangerously cold temperatures and impactful snowfall led to the closure of multiple school districts across the region as well as businesses and local government buildings. A few locations also saw infrastructure impacts such as pipes bursting in the region. Several counties also opened warming centers for the prolonged cold weather.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The highest snowfall amounts that occurred were 2.1 inches to the north-northwest of Farnsworth and an estimated three inches around Perryton. Then than two inches occurred in the western part of the county. A few high amounts may have occurred closer to the Lipscomb county line.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The only winter weather event of the season occurred January 23-25. A mix of sleet and snow fell across the region, but sleet was the predominant precipitation type. The highest sleet and snow totals were north of Interstate 20, and the highest freezing rain totals were in our far eastern counties. In addition to the wintry precipitation, bitterly cold air accompanied the system meeting Extreme Cold Warning criteria through the 27th. Unfortunately 8 deaths were reported with this event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sleet and snow totals up to 6.5 inches were reported across Cooke County. The highest sleet and snow totals were reported near Gainesville and Callisburg. Some damage occurred to an indoor arena near Gainesville with a metal structure collapsed due to the sleet and snow.
